title: 2 Kings 23:15–20
context: Josiah extends his reform to Bethel and the cities of Samaria, fulfilling the prophecy of 1 Kings 13 by burning bones on Jeroboam’s altar while sparing the tomb of the man of God.

verses.text: Moreover the altar that was at Bethel and the high place which Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, had made, even that altar and the high place he broke down; and he burned the high place and beat it to dust, and burned the Asherah.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah breaks down the altar and high place Jeroboam made at Bethel and burns the Asherah. Arminian readers see reform extending into the former northern kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah confronting the original site of northern apostasy. The mention of Jeroboam recalls the sin that shaped Israel’s history in 1 Kings 12.

verses.text: As Josiah turned himself, he spied the tombs that were there in the mountain; and he sent, and took the bones out of the tombs, and burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to the LORD’s word which the man of God proclaimed, who proclaimed these things.
verses.arminianNotes: He burns bones on the altar, “according to the LORD’s word which the man of God proclaimed.” Arminian readers see God’s word fulfilled through Josiah’s actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fulfillment of the prophecy in 1 Kings 13:2. The narrator highlights how God’s word, spoken long before, came to pass.

verses.text: Then he said, “What monument is that which I see?” The men of the city told him, “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these things that you have done against the altar of Bethel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah asks, “What monument is that which I see?” and learns it is the tomb of the man of God from Judah. Arminian readers see the past prophecy brought into view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word honored in the remembrance of the prophet. The exchange connects Josiah’s reforms with the prophetic history of 1 Kings 13.

verses.text: He said, “Let him be! Let no one move his bones.” So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: He says, “Let him be! Let no one move his bones.” Arminian readers see respect shown to the faithful prophet whose word had been fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see honor given to God’s messenger. The bones of the prophet from Samaria are also spared, as 1 Kings 13:31–32 anticipated.

verses.text: All the houses also of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the LORD to anger, Josiah took away, and did to them according to all the acts that he had done in Bethel.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah removes the high places in Samaria’s cities, as he had done in Bethel. Arminian readers see reform reaching across the former northern kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah’s zeal extending beyond Judah. The reference to provoking the LORD to anger reminds readers why these places were removed.

verses.text: He killed all the priests of the high places that were there, on the altars, and burned men’s bones on them; and he returned to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: He kills the priests of the high places there and burns human bones on the altars. Arminian readers note the severity of the action, which the narrator records without further comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse soberly and observe that the narrator presents it as part of the reform. Interpreters differ on how to relate this action to the law’s penalties for leading Israel into idolatry.
